heading: Networks can fit random labels with regularization and generalize without it
definition: weight decay, dropout and data augmentation do not stop networks from fitting random labels, and removing them does not by itself make generalization on true labels poor.
summary: Several independent groups reproduce random-label fitting with explicit regularization and useful generalization without it. This depends on the setting: regularization can suppress memorization in partially corrupted tasks.

suggested_status.by_scale: R2 for conditional results in <1B and parameter-count-unstated settings; toy partial-corruption settings also challenge unconditional nonprevention. No assigned level at 1–10B, 10–100B or >100B because V5 has no recorded coverage there.
suggested_status.reason: Independent-test records reproduce regularized fitting and useful generalization without conventional regularization: VGG weight-decay/augmentation experiments, small-Transformer fitting and the clean MNIST comparison. The unconditional wording is challenged by corrupted-algorithmic/MNIST suppression results. counts: versions.V5.studies_by_size and versions.V5.coverage_by_operation.training.by_size contain only '<1B' and 'not stated'; versions.V5.verdicts records supporting, scope-limiting and challenging evidence. R2 applies to the conditional observation, not universal immunity to regularization.
suggested_status.open_questions: Matched factorial tests with common fitting metrics, clean-label removal controls and longer fixed-recipe training would clarify the scope. Comparable experiments at billion-parameter scales would change the scale assessment.

source.title: Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization
source.authors: Chiyuan Zhang; Samy Bengio; Moritz Hardt; B. Recht; O. Vinyals

original_result.setup: Zhang et al. compared random-label fitting and true-label generalization with and without explicit regularizers.
original_result.result: On CIFAR10, Inception reached 100% random-label training accuracy with weight decay and 99.28–99.93% with augmentation; Alexnet failed to converge with weight decay. On true labels, Inception achieved 85.75% CIFAR10 test accuracy without augmentation or weight decay, while Inception V3 achieved 59.80% ImageNet test accuracy without augmentation, dropout or weight decay.
original_result.interpretation: This is the displayed original-result block, not a guarantee that the original tested every part of this claim.

wording_issues.phrase: do not stop networks from fitting random labels
wording_issues.issue: An unconditional reading exceeds the results. The original reports Alexnet failing to converge with weight decay; strong dropout suppresses noisy-label fitting. For quadratic MLPs on partially corrupted modular addition, dropout 0.0 yields coexistence with corrupted-label fitting observed; 0.3 yields partial inversion and partial fitting; 0.6 yields full inversion and absent corrupted-label memorization; 0.9 yields confusion and incomplete fitting. Separately, the MNIST four-layer ReLU MLP exhibits weight-decay-induced full inversion with absent corrupted-label memorization, very-high-weight-decay confusion, and increasing-dropout accuracy reductions; exact regularization and corruption settings for these MNIST outcomes are not stated in the extracted text. Finite-budget failures do not establish indefinite prevention.

Results on randomized subsets or partial corruption do not directly establish fitting or prevention when every training label is random. On MNIST with 80% uniformly incorrect labels, dropout 0.5 and weight decay 0.003 each permit acquisition of some noise information, but their fitting endpoints cannot be read. These information-acquisition results do not establish support, a limitation or a challenge to V5.

Successful comparisons often remove weight decay and dropout jointly while retaining augmentation, remove regularization only after early training, or retain minimal weight decay. These do not establish the effect of omitting all named regularizers from initialization.

Poor has no specified threshold. Inception with true labels has 89.05% test accuracy with random cropping and weight decay versus 85.75% without both; training accuracy is 100.0% in both conditions. ResNet18 on CIFAR10 after random-label pretraining, without momentum, reaches 56.024% test accuracy without augmentation or L2 versus 94.192% with both, qualifying the removal claim. For unregularized VGG19 on Caltech101 with 20 training samples per class, no dataset-specific measured chance baseline is stated; the paper's pooled baseline is fractional accuracy 0.01–0.005, equivalent to 1–0.5%. Above-chance accuracy does not establish comparable practical performance. Near-zero GPT-2 training–validation gaps measure overfitting and do not establish retained absolute held-out performance or support this clause.

wording_issues.phrase: data augmentation do not stop networks from fitting random labels
wording_issues.issue: Perfect fitting can refer specifically to original, unaugmented training images or a randomized subset. Original augmentation experiments instead report online minibatch accuracy with a changed decay factor. These endpoints do not establish perfect fitting over every augmented view.

The evidence mixes cross-entropy, natural and robust classification accuracy, zero subset classification error and positive perfect-fitting capacity. On MNIST with 75% symmetric corruption, the dropout CNN without AL2 has training cross-entropy 1.79 at epoch 700; training classification error is unreported, so incomplete classification fitting is undetermined. For TRADES on CIFAR-10 with random labels, natural training accuracy is 99.15–99.84% and robust training accuracy is 69.62–99.55% across the tested configurations; the first configuration's regularizer identity is ambiguous. Natural and robust accuracy describe different endpoints. Zero classification error does not establish zero loss; positive fitting capacity does not establish fitting an arbitrary larger dataset.

method_sensitivity.what: ResNet-18 weight-decay sweeps change fitting on partially randomized CIFAR-10. In quadratic modular addition at α = 0.5 and ξ = 0.35, decay 0 permits near-perfect training/test accuracy, 5 permits partial noise memorization, 15 suppresses it with 100% test accuracy, and 20 ends at random guessing. These are partial-corruption results. GELU modular-addition verdict prose reports fitting at λ = 0.0001 and rejection at 0.0005. In the digits MLP, strong decay gives 4.3% corrupted-label memorization at 10% noise and 32.3% at 60% noise, means over five seeds; the matched minimally regularized MLP gives 100%.

method_sensitivity.factor: Dropout strength, regularizer identity and fitting endpoint
method_sensitivity.what: ResNet-9 fits a 10% incorrect-label subset with dropout p = 0.4, while PreAct ResNet-18 with p = 0.7/0.8 suppresses fitting at higher corruption. Tuned dropout also hinders fully random-label fitting in small Alexnet-like CNNs. On MNIST with 75% symmetric corruption, without AL2, training cross-entropy at epoch 700 is 0.00 for the bare CNN, 0.02 with weight decay and 1.79 with dropout. Training classification error is unreported, so these losses do not establish incomplete classification fitting. Cross-study differences do not isolate dropout rate.

For randomized-label CIFAR100 WideResNet-28-10 at learning rate 0.01, decay 5 × 10^-4 and 50 epochs, corrected training errors are 29.04% for Stable-30, 17.24% for Spectral and 1.22% for Vanilla. Vanilla's near-zero error is an observed fitting result; Spectral and Stable-30 remain partially fitted. ResNet-110 remains incompletely fitted with and without decay at its 200-epoch endpoint.

Appendix E of the original preprint reports a stated decay-factor change from 0.95 to 0.999 and more training epochs for augmentation experiments. Reported accuracy is the global average of online minibatch accuracy on changing augmented samples. Encoder-projector perfect fitting is measured on original images. The partial-corruption CNN/residual-network experiments likewise evaluate randomized-subset classification on original images.

method_sensitivity.factor: Remaining augmentation, batch normalization and architecture depth
method_sensitivity.what: Removing weight decay and dropout preserves or improves generalization in the reported augmented All-CNN/WRN comparisons. The further study's reduced-data comparison covers original All-CNN and WRN-28-10; under heavier augmentation, removal generally improves accuracy, with a marginal regularization advantage for WRN on 50% of CIFAR-10. Its separate depth comparison reports improvement for deeper unregularized All-CNN variants and a slight drop for shallower ones. The broader augmentation study reports substantially worse All-CNN generalization without batch normalization when weight decay and dropout are removed while augmentation remains absent.

FlipUD(100%) can harm performance throughout training yet produce final accuracy above the clean baseline when restricted to the first third. Verdict prose also reports improved validation accuracy after switching weight decay off partway through training. These schedules do not establish omission effects from initialization.

Without augmentation or L2, ResNet18 CIFAR10 test accuracy is 84.838% from random initialization and 56.024% after random-label pretraining with vanilla SGD. With momentum, corresponding accuracies are 89.200% and 89.016%.

The original CIFAR10 weight-decay comparison reports fitting by Inception/MLPs and failed convergence by Alexnet. ImageNet Inception V3 reaches top-1 training accuracies of 91.18% with dropout and weight decay, 87.81% with weight decay alone and 95.20% with neither, with augmentation off. These ImageNet endpoints establish substantial incomplete fitting.

method_sensitivity.factor: Fitting capacity, training-set size and time
method_sensitivity.what: Weight decay reduces measured CNN perfect-fitting capacity while leaving some perfectly fitted random-label subsets. In the small-Transformer family with dropout 0.2 and decay 1.0, epochs to 99% random-label accuracy vary with capacity fraction; larger models memorize faster.

Without explicit regularization or augmentation, VGG19 Caltech101 test accuracy is 39.41% with 10 examples per class and 54.38% with 20. Separate ResNet018/ResNet101 experiments condition good unregularized generalization on sufficiently large sample sizes.
